podcast.title: "Charlie Brown" Extended Writing Process
podcast.body: Unlike the rapid creation of "Yakati Yak," the song "Charlie Brown" took significantly longer to develop. While Mike Stoller quickly came up with appropriate music, Jerry Lieber spent weeks agonizing before he found the title and conceived the basic idea for the lyrics, with Stoller assisting in the final refinement. "Charlie Brown took significantly longer to come up with than the ten minute that Yakite had taken."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Yakati Yak" Writing Process
podcast.body: The song "Yakati Yak" was famously written by Lieber and Stoller in about 10 minutes during a session at Lieber's house. Stoller was playing a piano rhythm that he thought might suit The Coasters when Lieber, from the kitchen, called out the first line: "take out the papers and the trash." Stoller immediately responded with "or you don't get no spending cash," and they rapidly traded lines to complete the song. "They traded off lines and had the song written in about 10 minutes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Classic Songwriting Split
podcast.body: Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller embodied a classic songwriting split: Lieber was primarily a lyricist who could not play an instrument but composed tunes in his head, while Stoller was an accomplished and sophisticated jazz pianist responsible for the music. Though they wrote together, they occasionally contributed ideas to each other's domain. "Lieber had started out as a songwriter who couldn't play an instrument or like music. He'd just written the mix down and remembered the tune in his head. While Stoller was already an accomplished and sophisticated jazz pianist by the time the two started collaborating."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Criticism Over Racial Portrayals
podcast.body: Lieber and Stoller faced criticism, notably from Johnny Otis, that their songs for The Coasters perpetuated racist stereotypes. Otis suggested they "dwelled entirely on a sort of street society," which, while perhaps reflecting a slice of life, wasn't typical of the black community. The controversy was heightened by their direction of black performers on songs written by white writers, drawing an analogy to the racial implications of "Amos 'n' Andy." "Johnny Otis in particular would make this criticism of the group's records, and it's one that must be taken seriously."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Dual Label Contracts
podcast.body: Lieber and Stoller held simultaneous contracts with two distinct labels. For RCA, they worked with white pop stars like Elvis Presley and Perry Como, a collaboration that produced some hits but was uncomfortable for both parties and ended after about a year. Concurrently, for Atlantic, they exclusively recorded with black performers they admired, such as Ruth Brown, LeVern Baker, and The Drifters, with The Coasters being their personal project. "They were contracted to RCA to work with white pop stars. Not just Elvis, though he was obviously important to them, but people like Perry Como, who were very far from Lieber and Stoller's normal music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Independent Writer-Producers
podcast.body: Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller had a unique and unusual setup for the 1950s, operating as independent writer-producers. They were effectively under contract to two different labels, RCA and Atlantic, whose markets and audiences did not significantly overlap. "They were independent writer producers, an unusual state in itself in the 1950s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Jewish Identity and Black Culture Involvement
podcast.body: In the context of the racial stereotyping criticism, it was noted that Lieber and Stoller were Jewish, and at the time, were "only on the borders of whiteness themselves." They were also deeply involved in black culture. Despite this, they claimed on several occasions that their songs were not specifically about black people. "What can I say if it makes a difference that Lieber and Stoller would Jewish, and so were only on the borders of whiteness themselves at the time, or that they were deeply involved in black culture themselves?"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mentored Phil Spector
podcast.body: Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller played a significant role in the early career of Phil Spector. As a favor to their mentor Lester Sill, they took Spector, who was a huge admirer and wanted to learn from them, under their wing. They signed him to a publishing contract, provided him with jobs as a session guitarist, and even allowed him to stay in their office or Lieber's spare room for a period. "So as a favour to Sill, and even though they found this like the kid once he got to New New York, they signed him to a publishing contract, gave him jobs as a session guitarist, and even let him sleep in their office or in Leibor's spare room for a while."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Pseudonym "Elmo Glick"
podcast.body: Lieber and Stoller sometimes used the pseudonym "Elmo Glick." This name was credited as the writer for The Coasters' song "Shopping for Clothes" because they were unable to identify the original writer, Kent Harris, at the time of its recording. "They'd been unable to find out who had written it, so it just quit as it, to Elmo Glick, a pseudonym they sometimes used."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Studio Roles
podcast.body: In the studio, Mike Stoller was responsible for writing the parts for the musicians and playing the piano, while Jerry Lieber supervised from the control room. This division of labor contributed to The Coasters becoming a "hit making machine" with their new lineup. "Stoller would write the parts for the musicians and play the piano, while Lieber supervised in the control room."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
